planting.note: Start from seed after the last frost or set out nursery divisions in spring so plants establish a strong root system before their first winter.

directions: Fatal Attraction stands apart from ordinary purple coneflower by pairing rich magenta-purple ray petals with near-black stems and calyxes, giving the whole plant a dramatic two-tone silhouette even before the dark orange-brown cone opens. Grow it in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; overly rich or wet ground softens the stem color and can shorten the clump's lifespan. Deadhead spent blooms to extend flowering into late summer, or leave the last flush standing so the spiny seed heads feed goldfinches through winter. The strong dark stems make this cultivar a favorite for cut-flower gardeners who want contrast without relying on unusual petal color alone.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant divisions in spring once the soil has warmed, giving roots a full season to establish before winter dormancy.

directions: Fragrant Angel produces large, pure white, horizontally held ray petals around a bronze-orange cone, on taller, sturdier stems than many white coneflower cultivars, so it tends to need less staking in open borders. As the name suggests, the blooms carry a noticeably sweeter scent than typical Echinacea purpurea, making it a good choice near patios or cutting gardens where fragrance matters. Plant in full sun and average, well-drained soil; established clumps are drought-tolerant and rarely need supplemental water once rooted. Leave faded flower heads in place over winter for songbird forage and reseed a few volunteers if you want the patch to slowly expand.

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost, or start indoors 6-8 weeks earlier for earlier bloom.

directions: Irish Eyes replaces the typical dark chocolate-brown cone of black-eyed Susan with a glowing lime-green center, so the golden-yellow ray petals appear to float around a genuinely green eye rather than a black one. Grown as a fast, reliable warm-season annual (or short-lived perennial in mild climates), it thrives in average to lean soil and full sun and tolerates heat and short dry spells better than most annual bedding flowers. Deadhead regularly to keep new buds coming through summer and into fall, and use it as a color-echo companion for other green-centered or lime-toned flowers in a cutting bed. Its unusual eye color makes it a conversation piece in mixed borders where standard Rudbeckia hirta is already common.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after the last frost, or start indoors 6-8 weeks early for a head start on bloom.

directions: Sonora carries an unusually wide mahogany-red band circling each ray petal's base, tipped in bright gold, giving the large 5-6 inch blooms a bold two-color banded look distinct from the mostly solid-gold black-eyed Susans typically grown from seed. Its branching, compact habit produces heavy bud counts on relatively short stems, making it well suited to containers and the front of sunny borders as well as cut-flower rows. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun; this warm-season plant germinates and flowers quickly from seed, usually blooming within ten weeks of sowing. Deadhead to prolong the show through summer heat, when many other bedding annuals begin to fade.

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost, or start indoors 6-8 weeks earlier for earlier bloom on this compact double-flowered selection.

directions: Maya is a fully double, pompom-flowered black-eyed Susan whose dense golden-orange blooms show little to no visible central disc, a striking departure from the single daisy form most gardeners associate with Rudbeckia hirta. Its compact, uniform habit keeps plants tidy in beds, borders, and containers without staking, and the sturdy stems hold up well as cut flowers. Grow in full sun and average, well-drained soil; this fast-blooming warm-season annual germinates readily from seed and flowers within about three months of sowing. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep the compact plants producing new buds through the heat of summer.
